Folly Road (SC-171) is the lifeline of James Island — and the primary route to Folly Beach, one of the most popular beach destinations in the Charleston area. Every day, thousands of James Island residents, commuters, and beachgoers funnel onto this single corridor, creating traffic conditions that produce car accidents with alarming regularity. During summer months and holiday weekends, the volume surges even higher as tourists unfamiliar with the road compete for space with local traffic.

According to the South Carolina Department of Transportation, the five-mile stretch of Folly Road from Maybank Highway to Old Folly Beach Road recorded 2,103 vehicle crashes, 15 pedestrian crashes and 21 bicycle crashes from January 2018 to December 2022 — 525 of them causing injury and six fatal — and SCDOT selected it for a federally funded road safety audit. Charleston County as a whole logged 15,802 collisions in 2024, second in the state, according to the South Carolina Department of Public Safety. The road's unique combination of high volume, limited alternative routes, dense commercial development, and the bottleneck effect of being the only road to Folly Beach creates a crash environment that endangers drivers, passengers, cyclists, and pedestrians every day.

Folly Road: James Island's Main Corridor

Folly Road runs roughly seven miles from the James Island Connector (SC-30) near downtown Charleston to the entrance of Folly Beach. Along the way, it passes through the commercial heart of James Island — shopping centers, restaurants, gas stations, medical offices, schools, and churches — before transitioning into the more residential and marshy approach to Folly Beach.

The road carries a staggering traffic load for its design. Through James Island, Folly Road is a five-lane road — two travel lanes each way and a continuous center turn lane, with no median — that narrows to one lane in each direction on the approach to Folly Beach. The sheer volume of traffic — particularly the combination of through traffic heading to Folly Beach and local traffic making short trips between businesses and neighborhoods — creates constant congestion and conflict points. Folly Road carried about 33,000 vehicles a day at Harbor View Road and 29,800 at Fort Johnson Road in 2019 (BCDCOG counts), and on spring and summer weekends beach traffic backs up on top of that.

Why Folly Road Is One of Charleston's Most Crash-Prone Roads

No Alternative Route to Folly Beach

Folly Road is the only road on and off Folly Beach, and while Riverland Drive, Harbor View Road and Camp Road carry some James Island traffic, none of them can absorb Folly Road's volume. This funneling effect concentrates traffic — commuters, commercial vehicles, tourists, school buses, cyclists — onto a single corridor, maximizing the opportunities for crashes.

Tourist and Unfamiliar Drivers

During summer months, a significant percentage of drivers on Folly Road are tourists who do not know the road, are unfamiliar with local driving patterns, are distracted by GPS navigation, or are looking for specific businesses and turn-offs. Unfamiliar drivers brake suddenly, make unexpected turns, and miss signals — all behaviors that contribute to rear-end and sideswipe crashes.

Dense Commercial Development

The central section of Folly Road is lined with commercial driveways on both sides. Every driveway is a conflict point where turning vehicles cross the path of through traffic. Left turns across traffic into businesses and shopping centers are a primary cause of T-bone collisions on Folly Road.

Speed Transitions

Folly Road is posted at 45 mph across most of James Island, then drops sharply on the approach to Folly Beach, where the city won SCDOT approval in 2018 to post 25 mph inside its limits. Drivers who fail to notice these transitions or who are impatient with slower traffic in the lower-speed zones create speed differential hazards.

Cyclist and Pedestrian Exposure

Despite the high traffic volume, Folly Road is a popular cycling route (it carries on-street bike lanes on portions of the corridor and across the rebuilt Folly River bridges, with gaps in between) and pedestrians cross frequently to reach bus stops, restaurants, and shops. The limited shoulder width and inconsistent sidewalk coverage put vulnerable road users in close proximity to high-speed traffic.

Flooding and Weather

James Island is low-lying and flood-prone. Folly Road floods regularly during heavy rain and king tides, creating hazardous driving conditions — standing water, reduced visibility, and hydroplaning.

Where Folly Road's Conflict Points Are

  • Folly Road and Maybank Highway intersection — one of the busiest intersections on James Island, where traffic from Johns Island merges with Folly Road traffic; heavy turning movements add conflict, and it marks the northern end of the five-mile stretch SCDOT singled out for its safety audit
  • Folly Road near Camp Road — the commercial core of James Island with dense driveways, high pedestrian activity, and constant turning conflicts
  • The James Island Connector merge — where the high-speed connector (SC-30) feeds into Folly Road, creating speed differential hazards as highway-speed traffic meets surface-street congestion
  • Folly Road approaching the Folly River bridge — the road narrows and traffic compresses as it approaches the bridge to Folly Beach, creating tailgating and rear-end collision risks
  • Sol Legare Road intersection — where the five-lane commercial corridor gives way to the two-lane marsh section, so drivers still carrying 45 mph meet turning traffic from the Sol Legare neighborhood

Common Types of Car Accidents on Folly Road

Rear-End Collisions

One of the most common crash types on Folly Road. Stop-and-go traffic, sudden braking for red lights, and congestion backups — particularly during beach traffic — create conditions where distracted or following-too-closely drivers rear-end the vehicle ahead.

Left-Turn T-Bone Crashes

Drivers turning left across oncoming traffic into businesses, shopping centers, and side streets risk high-energy broadside collisions. On Folly Road, where gaps in oncoming traffic are short and sight lines are often obstructed by vehicles in adjacent lanes, left-turn crashes are particularly dangerous. T-bone collisions deliver force to the weakest part of the struck vehicle — the side — where there is minimal crash protection.

Sideswipe and Lane-Change Crashes

Impatient drivers changing lanes in congested traffic, vehicles drifting across lane markings, and merging conflicts at the James Island Connector produce sideswipe crashes. While often lower-severity, sideswipes can cause vehicles to spin into oncoming traffic or off the road.

Bicycle and Pedestrian Crashes

Cyclists sharing Folly Road with motor vehicles and pedestrians crossing at unsignalized locations are at high risk. The narrow shoulders and absence of protected bike lanes on most of Folly Road mean that bicycle accidents on this corridor tend to be severe. SCDOT's safety audit counted 21 bicycle and 15 pedestrian crashes on the corridor between 2018 and 2022, and three of its six fatal crashes killed pedestrians.

DUI Crashes

Folly Road is the only road home from Folly Beach's bars and restaurants, and impaired driving is a statewide problem: an alcohol-impaired driver was involved in 40% of South Carolina's traffic deaths in 2024, according to the SCDPS Traffic Collision Fact Book. In Charleston County, 20 of the 57 fatal collisions that year happened between 9 p.m. and 3 a.m. Impaired drivers are more likely to cross the center line, run red lights, and fail to react to stopped traffic.

Injuries From Folly Road Crashes

The speed and traffic volume on Folly Road produce injuries ranging from whiplash to fatal:

  • Traumatic brain injuries — from high-speed impacts, T-bone collisions, and pedestrian/cyclist crashes
  • Spinal cord injuries — herniated discs, compression fractures, and paralysis from rear-end and broadside impacts
  • Broken bones — fractures of the wrist, arm, hip, pelvis, and legs from collision forces
  • Internal injuries — organ damage from seatbelt loading and steering wheel impact in frontal and T-bone crashes
  • Whiplash and soft tissue injuries — neck and back injuries from rear-end collisions, which can cause chronic pain lasting months or years
  • Wrongful death — SCDOT counted six fatal crashes on Folly Road between 2018 and 2022, half of them involving pedestrians

Who Is Liable for an Accident on Folly Road?

  • The at-fault driver — for distracted driving, tailgating, running red lights, DUI, failure to yield on left turns, or unsafe lane changes
  • Commercial vehicle operators and employers — truck drivers, delivery drivers, and their employers may share liability when commercial vehicles are involved
  • Government entities — SCDOT, which owns Folly Road, the City of Charleston, which maintains signals on its sections, and Charleston County may bear responsibility for road design defects, missing turn lanes, or signs and signals left uncorrected after notice under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-10 et seq.). These claims must be filed within two years (S.C. Code § 15-78-110), damages are capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence with no punitive damages (S.C. Code § 15-78-120), and discretionary decisions are immune (S.C. Code § 15-78-60)
  • Vehicle and parts manufacturers — for defective brakes, tires, steering, or safety systems that contributed to the crash
  • Bars and restaurants — South Carolina has no dram-shop act, but an establishment that knowingly serves a visibly intoxicated patron violates S.C. Code §§ 61-4-580 and 61-6-2220, which the courts treat as negligence per se (Tobias v. Sports Club; Hartfield v. Getaway Lounge & Grill), so a Folly Beach bar that over-serves a driver who then crashes on Folly Road may share liability

South Carolina changed these rules for claims arising after 1 January 2026. The 2025 Act narrowed the alcohol exception in S.C. Code § 15-38-15 and created § 61-2-147, under which an establishment can be jointly and severally liable for fifty percent of a plaintiff’s actual damages where a verdict is returned against both it and a driver charged with DUI — what South Carolina’s 2026 liquor liability law changed.

South Carolina's Comparative Fault Rule and Folly Road Crashes

South Carolina follows a modified comparative fault rule (Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co.). You can recover damages if your fault is less than 51%. Your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault.

Insurance companies handling Folly Road crashes frequently argue that the injured driver was following too closely, was distracted, or failed to take evasive action. In the congested, stop-and-go environment of Folly Road — where close following distances are often unavoidable and sudden stops are constant — an experienced attorney can counter these arguments with traffic analysis and accident reconstruction evidence.

Filing Deadlines for Charleston Area Car Accident Claims

South Carolina provides three years from the date of the accident for personal injury claims (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) and three years from the date of death for wrongful death claims (S.C. Code § 15-51-20). A claim against SCDOT, the City of Charleston or Charleston County under the Tort Claims Act must be filed within two years (S.C. Code § 15-78-110).

Critical evidence on Folly Road disappears quickly — traffic camera footage, business surveillance video, and vehicle data are all time-sensitive. Contacting an attorney within the first few days preserves your ability to secure this evidence.

What to Do After an Accident on Folly Road

  1. Move to safety — Folly Road's heavy traffic makes secondary crashes a real risk; move vehicles off the road if possible
  2. Call 911 — request police and medical assistance; a police report is critical evidence
  3. Seek medical attention — even seemingly minor symptoms can indicate serious injury; document everything within 24 hours
  4. Document the scene — photograph vehicle damage, road conditions, traffic signals, skid marks, and your injuries
  5. Exchange information — get the other driver's name, insurance, license plate, and phone number
  6. Identify witnesses — nearby business employees and other drivers may have seen the crash
  7. Do not give recorded statements to the other driver's insurance company without consulting an attorney
  8. Contact a car accident lawyer — the sooner evidence preservation letters are sent, the stronger your case

How a James Island Car Accident Lawyer Can Help

Crashes on Folly Road often involve complex liability questions — tourist drivers with out-of-state insurance, DUI defendants, possible government liability for road design, and commercial vehicle involvement. A Charleston car accident lawyer from Roden Law can:

  • Preserve critical evidence — secure traffic camera and business surveillance footage before it is overwritten
  • Investigate the crash thoroughly — retain accident reconstruction experts, review police reports, and analyze Folly Road's design and signal timing
  • Handle out-of-state insurance companies — tourist-involved crashes often mean dealing with unfamiliar insurers from other states
  • Pursue DUI-related claims — in crashes caused by impaired drivers, pursue both the driver and, where applicable, the establishment that over-served them
  • Maximize your compensation — ensure that medical bills, lost wages, future treatment, and pain and suffering are fully valued

From our Charleston office, Roden Law represents crash victims throughout James Island, Folly Beach, and the greater Charleston area. We handle every car accident case on a contingency-fee basis — you pay nothing unless we recover compensation for you.

If you have been injured in an accident on Folly Road, call us today at (843) 790-8999 or 1-844-RESULTS for a free consultation.

If you drive through North Charleston, you probably already know the intersection of Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26 feels dangerous. What you may not know is that data confirms it: 629 crashes were recorded there between 2011 and 2015 — roughly one every three days, and more than at any other intersection in Berkeley, Charleston or Dorchester counties. Statewide it ranked second for 2011–2015, behind I-20 at US-176 in Columbia; in 2024 it ranked fifth. Notably, none of those 629 crashes was fatal, though 181 people were injured (Post and Courier 2017 analysis of preliminary South Carolina Department of Public Safety data, 2011–2015).

As personal injury lawyers who handle crash cases from this intersection regularly, we've seen the injuries it produces — from T-bone collisions to rear-end chain reactions. Here's what makes this intersection so crash-prone and what you can do to protect yourself.

The Numbers: Ashley Phosphate & I-26 by the Data

Let's put the danger in perspective:

  • 2024 (latest state data): 174 collisions at I-26 and Ashley Phosphate Road — second in Charleston County and the tri-county behind I-26 at US-78 (190) and fifth statewide. No one was killed; 39 people were injured, and 148 of the crashes were property damage only (SCDPS 2024 Fact Book)

5 Reasons This Intersection Is So Crash-Prone

1. Interstate Speed Meets Red Lights

Vehicles exiting I-26 at Exit 209 come off the interstate and reach a signal at Ashley Phosphate Road a short distance later. Drivers who are distracted, unfamiliar with the area, or simply carrying too much speed can run the red light. The resulting T-bone collision with a vehicle legally entering the intersection produces catastrophic force.

2. Complex Left-Turn Movements

Ashley Phosphate Road has multiple left-turn lanes in both directions. Vehicles turning left must cross three lanes of opposing traffic on a seven-lane road. The margin for error is razor-thin — misjudge the gap by even one second and the result is a violent head-on-angle collision combining the energy of both vehicles.

3. Commercial Density Around the Interchange

Shopping centers, hotels, gas stations, and restaurants line Ashley Phosphate Road around the interchange. Drivers aren't just passing through — they're turning, merging, exiting parking lots, and hunting for entrances. This constant churn of turning movements creates unpredictable conflicts that even attentive drivers struggle to anticipate.

4. Drivers Who Fail to Yield

According to the SCDPS 2024 Fact Book, failure to yield the right of way was the leading contributing factor in Charleston County collisions in 2024. Where off-ramp traffic, left turns, and driveway traffic all meet, one driver who fails to yield can cause a collision.

5. Volume Has Outgrown Design Capacity

According to SCDOT, traffic on Ashley Phosphate Road has grown beyond the recommended level for two-way left-turn lanes. North Charleston's population reached about 129,245 in July 2025 (Census estimate), and I-26 carries 170,500 vehicles a day between Ashley Phosphate Road and Aviation Avenue, with 65,000 more on Ashley Phosphate Road (SCDOT, 2025).

Common Crash Types at Busy Interchanges

Crash TypeTypical CauseCommon Injuries
T-bone (side impact)Red-light running from I-26 off-rampPelvic fractures, internal organs, TBI
Left-turn collisionMisjudged gap in opposing trafficHead-on force injuries, chest trauma
Rear-end chainSudden stops at signal during congestionWhiplash, disc herniation, concussion
Pedestrian strikeTurning vehicles vs. pedestrians in crosswalkFractures, traumatic brain injury, fatality

What Should Be Done About It

Traffic engineers have tools that could reduce the crash frequency at Ashley Phosphate/I-26:

  • Protected left-turn signals — Eliminating permissive left turns during high-volume periods
  • Red-light cameras — A federal study found about 25% fewer right-angle crashes but about 15% more rear-end crashes; South Carolina law currently bars local camera ticketing (S.C. Code § 56-5-710(B))
  • Extended deceleration lanes — Giving I-26 exit traffic more distance to slow before reaching the signal
  • Restricted access management — Reducing the number of driveway access points near the intersection
  • Raised medians — SCDOT broke ground in July 2025 on an Ashley Phosphate Road safety project (Rivers Avenue to Dorchester Road) adding raised medians, high-visibility crosswalks, and better lighting

SCDOT has begun with that raised-median project; until more of these improvements are in place, crashes here are likely to continue.

What to Do If You're Injured at This Intersection

  1. Call 911 — Get a police report documenting the scene, signal state, and contributing factors
  2. Get medical treatment immediately — Trident Medical Center (9330 Medical Plaza Dr) is the closest trauma facility
  3. Photograph everything — Signal positions, vehicle damage, intersection layout, your injuries
  4. Get witness contacts — Nearby businesses may have seen the crash; get names and numbers before they leave
  5. Do not give recorded statements — The other driver's insurance company will try to minimize your claim
  6. Contact a lawyer — A Charleston car accident lawyer can pull traffic camera footage, obtain the signal timing report, and preserve evidence before it's lost

Your Legal Rights Under South Carolina Law

If you were injured at Ashley Phosphate Road and I-26:

  • Statute of limitations: 3 years from the date of injury to file suit (S.C. Code § 15-3-530)
  • Comparative fault: You can recover damages if you were less than 51% at fault — your award is reduced by your percentage of responsibility
  • Government liability: If a malfunctioning or defective traffic signal contributed to your crash and the responsible agency knew or should have known and did not fix it, SCDOT or another agency may be liable under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act (S.C. Code § 15-78-60(15)) — highway design itself is immune, and damages are capped at $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence (S.C. Code § 15-78-120). 1. Interstate Speed Meets Red Lights

Vehicles exiting I-26 at Exit 209 come off the interstate and reach a signal at Ashley Phosphate Road a short distance later. Drivers who are distracted, unfamiliar with the area, or simply carrying too much speed can run the red light. The resulting T-bone collision with a vehicle legally entering the intersection produces catastrophic force.

2. Complex Left-Turn Movements

Ashley Phosphate Road has multiple left-turn lanes in both directions. Vehicles turning left must cross three lanes of opposing traffic on a seven-lane road. The margin for error is razor-thin — misjudge the gap by even one second and the result is a violent head-on-angle collision combining the energy of both vehicles.

3. Commercial Density Around the Interchange

Shopping centers, hotels, gas stations, and restaurants line Ashley Phosphate Road around the interchange. Drivers aren't just passing through — they're turning, merging, exiting parking lots, and hunting for entrances. This constant churn of turning movements creates unpredictable conflicts that even attentive drivers struggle to anticipate. Citing South Carolina Department of Transportation traffic data, Live 5 News reported in July 2026 that four of Charleston County's five deadliest roads are in North Charleston: Rivers Avenue, Dorchester Road, Ashley Phosphate Road and Remount Road.

4. Drivers Who Fail to Yield

According to the SCDPS 2024 Fact Book, failure to yield the right of way was the leading contributing factor in Charleston County collisions in 2024. Where off-ramp traffic, left turns, and driveway traffic all meet, one driver who fails to yield can cause a collision.

Interstate 16: Port Traffic and High-Speed Interchanges

Interstate 16 stretches 167 miles from Savannah to Macon, and the Savannah-area segment of this highway has a history of fatal collisions: federal data count about 14 fatal crashes on I-16 in Chatham County from 2020 through 2024. Key danger zones on I-16:

  • The I-16/Chatham Parkway interchange sits on a stretch of I-16 that carried about 60,000 vehicles a day in 2019 (a GDOT count reported by AARoads), and GDOT has added ramp meters there to manage merging traffic. Short merge ramps can force vehicles to enter the highway at dangerous speed differentials.
  • The I-16/I-95 junction is being rebuilt by GDOT's 16@95 project to ease a long-standing bottleneck, but it still funnels long-distance interstate traffic into local commuter traffic, and its merging zones can produce rear-end and sideswipe crashes.
  • The I-16/I-516 split west of downtown Savannah confuses unfamiliar drivers and can produce sideswipe crashes as vehicles attempt last-second lane changes.

Truck accidents on I-16 are particularly devastating. A fully loaded tractor-trailer traveling at highway speed can weigh 80,000 pounds, and the force of a collision between a commercial truck and a passenger vehicle at highway speed frequently produces traumatic brain injuries, spinal cord injuries, and fatalities. If a truck driver's fatigue, distraction, or impairment caused your crash on I-16, you may have claims against both the driver and the trucking company.

Interstate 95 is the East Coast's main north-south interstate, and it runs directly through the Savannah metropolitan area. Federal crash data bears that out: across 2022–2024, I-95 recorded more fatal crashes than any US interstate except I-10 — 924 fatal crashes and 1,020 deaths nationally, second of 222 interstate designations (NHTSA Fatality Analysis Reporting System, annual files, accessed 25 August 2026). Why I-95 is so dangerous near Savannah:

  • Speed and volume: Vehicles traveling at up to 70 mph in dense traffic leave little margin for error. A momentary distraction at highway speed can result in a catastrophic crash.

Abercorn Street is one of the deadliest roads in the City of Savannah: from 2020 through 2024, about 11 fatal crashes on Abercorn inside the city killed 12 people, tied with U.S. 17 for the most deaths of any city road (NHTSA FARS).   • Speeding: Excessive speed reduces stopping distance and dramatically increases crash severity.   • Truck driver fatigue: Federal hours-of-service regulations limit how long commercial truck drivers can operate without rest, capping driving at 11 hours after 10 hours off duty (49 C.F.R. § 395.3). Fatigued truck drivers on I-16 and I-95 pose an extreme danger to everyone sharing the road.

Statute of limitations: Georgia gives accident victims two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33.

Comparative fault: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule allowing recovery if you are less than 50% at fault, with your award reduced by your percentage of responsibility.

Commercial vehicle regulations: Truck accidents on I-16, I-95, and I-516 may involve violations of the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations governing driver hours of service, vehicle maintenance, cargo securement, and driver qualifications. Wrongful death: When a highway crash kills a victim, Georgia's wrongful death statute (O.C.G.A. §§ 51-4-1, 51-4-2) allows the surviving spouse (or, if there is none, the children) to recover the full value of the decedent's life; if neither survives, the parents may recover under O.C.G.A. § 19-7-1.

  1. Move to safety if possible. Highway crashes create extreme secondary collision risks. If your vehicle is drivable, move it to the shoulder. Turn on hazard lights and stay behind the guardrail.
  2. Call 911 immediately. Georgia law requires reporting accidents involving injuries. Highway crashes often require specialized response including fire rescue and traffic control.
  3. Seek medical treatment even if you think your injuries are minor. Adrenaline can mask pain from serious injuries like concussions, internal bleeding, and soft tissue damage.
  4. Document the scene with photographs if it is safe to do so. Capture vehicle positions, road conditions, weather, skid marks, and any debris patterns.
  5. Do not discuss fault with other drivers or insurance representatives at the scene.
  6. Contact a Savannah car accident lawyer before providing recorded statements to any insurance company.

How a Savannah Car Accident Lawyer Can Help

Highway crash cases — especially those involving commercial trucks on I-16, I-95, and I-516 — are among the most complex personal injury claims.   • Obtain and analyze electronic logging device (ELD) records, dashcam footage, and vehicle black box data
  • Investigate whether federal trucking regulations were violated, including hours-of-service rules and maintenance requirements
  • Document the full scope of your injuries and damages, including future medical needs and lost earning capacity
  • Negotiate aggressively with insurance companies and take your case to trial in the State or Superior Court of Chatham County if necessary

Roden Law represents highway crash victims across Savannah and Southeast Georgia on a contingency fee basis. Fees and costs apply only upon successful recovery. No fees or costs with no recovery. With over $300 million recovered for our clients and a 4.9-star average client rating, we have the resources and experience to take on the largest trucking companies and insurance carriers.

Injured on one of Savannah's high-crash roads? Contact Roden Law today for a free consultation. Call (912) 303-5850 or 1-844-RESULTS.

Claims against the City of Savannah require written notice within six months (O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5), and counties cannot be sued unless a statute allows it (O.C.G.A. § 36-1-4), with claims due within 12 months (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1).

Georgia Laws for Accident Victims

Statute of limitations: Georgia gives accident victims two years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33.

Comparative fault: Under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule allowing recovery if you are less than 50% at fault, with your award reduced by your percentage of responsibility.

Commercial vehicle regulations: Truck accidents on I-16, I-95, and I-516 may involve violations of the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations governing driver hours of service, vehicle maintenance, cargo securement, and driver qualifications. These violations can serve as powerful evidence of negligence in your injury claim.

Wrongful death: When a highway crash kills a victim, Georgia's wrongful death statute (O.C.G.A. §§ 51-4-1, 51-4-2) allows the surviving spouse (or, if there is none, the children) to recover the full value of the decedent's life; if neither survives, the parents may recover under O.C.G.A. § 19-7-1.

What to Do After a Highway Crash in Savannah

  1. Move to safety if possible. Highway crashes create extreme secondary collision risks. If your vehicle is drivable, move it to the shoulder. Turn on hazard lights and stay behind the guardrail.
  2. Call 911 immediately. Georgia law requires reporting accidents involving injuries. Highway crashes often require specialized response including fire rescue and traffic control.
  3. Document the truck if one was involved: photograph its company name, the USDOT number on the cab door, the trailer number and the cargo type. They identify the carrier and its insurer.
  4. Seek medical treatment even if you think your injuries are minor. Adrenaline can mask pain from serious injuries like concussions, internal bleeding, and soft tissue damage. Memorial Health University Medical Center in Savannah is the region's Level I trauma center (Georgia Department of Public Health).
  5. Document the scene with photographs if it is safe to do so. Capture vehicle positions, road conditions, weather, skid marks, and any debris patterns.
  6. Do not discuss fault with other drivers or insurance representatives at the scene.
  7. Contact a Savannah car accident lawyer before providing recorded statements to any insurance company.
